html:
A script used to write Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and dozens of other languages across Eurasia, by some 250 million people. It was created in the First Bulgarian Empire around the 890s, probably at the school of Preslav.

It is named after Saint Cyril, who with his brother Methodius made the earlier Glagolitic script in the 860s for their mission to Moravia. Their disciples carried the Slavonic liturgy to newly Christian Bulgaria. There, scholars built a simpler script from the Greek alphabet, adding letters for Slavic sounds, and it soon replaced Glagolitic in most places.

Cyrillic spread with Orthodox Christianity to Serbia and, after the baptism of Rus', to Kyiv and Russia. Peter the Great simplified it in 1708. The Russian Empire and the Soviet Union brought it to many languages that are not Slavic, from Kazakh to Mongolian. Since Bulgaria joined in 2007 it has been an official script of the European Union.
